target_customer: Pharmaceutical partners and, later, kidney disease patients; today pharma sponsors fund preclinical work
problem: Almost no clinical stage genetic medicines target the kidney or pancreas, which the company attributes mainly to a lack of efficient delivery vehicles. Nephrogen engineers AAV delivery vehicles and promoters for those organs.
business_model: Preclinical biotech funded by pharma sponsors and investors, aiming to develop one-time gene therapies and license delivery vehicles
product_category: Gene therapy delivery platform (AAV) for kidney and pancreas diseases

founders.name: Demetri Maxim
education: Stanford, computational biology (company page: Stanford computational biologist; a search summary says graduate student)
founders.background_notes: Company page says he has researched kidney disease since age 14 and aims to cure genetic kidney disease by 2035.

founders.name: Vivek Bhalla
prior_employers: Stanford University (associate professor of medicine, nephrologist, director of the Stanford Hypertension Center)
founders.background_notes: Company page and the National Kidney Foundation release both call him a co-founder.

technical_complexity.rationale: Engineering tissue-specific AAV vectors with machine learning and in vivo screening, then proving delivery in intact human kidneys, is research-grade work that needs preclinical and regulatory development.

defensibility.rationale: Proprietary vectors and screening data would be hard to copy if validated, but the platform is preclinical and the claims are not yet independently confirmed; the company page shows no patents.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: The NKF release says only one program designed to target kidney cells is known to have entered clinical trials, so no well resourced player was building the same wedge in opened sources.

market_need_then: Kidney disease affects 1 in 7 Americans per the YC page, with no approved gene-based therapies for the kidney or pancreas; the company says 903 clinical stage genetic medicines include almost none aimed at these organs.

identity.logo: Not confirmed by any source opened
identity.voice_and_tone: Mission driven and confident with focus on patient impact and a goal to cure genetic kidney disease by 2035

branding.brand_signature: NeFIND platform name and the cure by 2035 mission
branding.community_and_virality: Featured in a TechCrunch Disrupt 2025 piece; no merch or community found.

brand_strength.rationale: Clear descriptive name tied to the kidney, with scattered press, but little sourced brand recognition.

outcome_analysis: Nephrogen is an early stage preclinical Stanford spinout that has raised little equity publicly: TechCrunch said in October 2025 it was raising a 4 million dollar seed and the National Kidney Foundation Innovation Fund invested in October 2026. Non-dilutive money from pharma sponsors supports the work. Outcome is open and depends on proving delivery data and raising larger rounds.
notes: Batch conflict: the directory says Summer 2020 and a launch date in 2022, while TechCrunch and the YC page say the company was founded in 2022; founded_year follows the press and as_of in competition follows the directory batch. Search summaries disagree on the YC batch (Winter or Summer 2020). Funding figures from aggregators are unverified: CB Insights 700K over 6 rounds, others 775K plus a 325K NIH grant, a 2.0M or 4M seed. Pharma sponsors named on the company site by logo only (EMD, Bayer, Otsuka, BMS, Chiesi, Alnylam); the YC page lists Merck KGaA, Novartis and BMS; amounts not stated. No dated competitor sources found; Estuary Biotherapeutics appeared only in an undated search summary. Founder education and employers are thin.
